questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Identify the INCORRECT statement
options: A process will always be spontaneous at all temperatures, if T$\Delta$S is positive
For spontaneous process $([\Delta H_{system} - T\Delta S_{system}]) \lt  0$
At 273K, for the transition Ice$(s) \longrightarrow$ Water $(l)$, $\Delta$G = 0
Entropy is an extensive property and state function
questions.solution:
$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$

For a process to be spontaneous at all temperatures, $\Delta G$ must be negative at all temperatures. This is possible only when $\Delta H \lt 0$ and $\Delta S \gt 0$. If $\Delta S \gt 0$ (meaning $T\Delta S$ is positive) but $\Delta H \gt 0$, the process will be non-spontaneous at low temperatures where $\Delta H \gt T\Delta S$. Thus, a positive $T\Delta S$ alone does not guarantee spontaneity at all temperatures.

For a spontaneous process at constant temperature and pressure, $\Delta G_{system} = \Delta H_{system} - T\Delta S_{system} \lt 0$.

At $273$ K, ice and water are in equilibrium, so $\Delta G = 0$.

Entropy is an extensive property as it depends on the mass of the system, and it is a state function as it depends only on the initial and final states.

Answer: A process will always be spontaneous at all temperatures, if T$\Delta$S is positive

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The standard enthalpies of formation of CH_4$(g), CO_2$(g) and H_2$O(l) are $-74.8$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, $-393.5$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ and $-285.8$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ respectively. Then the enthalpy change for the given reaction in kJ mol$^{-1}$ will be: \\ $2\text{CH}_4(g) + 4\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2(g) + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)
questions.solution:
The enthalpy of reaction is calculated using the standard enthalpies of formation of the products and reactants.

$\Delta_{r}H^{\circ} = \sum \Delta_{f}H^{\circ}(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta_{f}H^{\circ}(\text{reactants})$

For the given reaction:

$\Delta_{r}H^{\circ} = [2 \Delta_{f}H^{\circ}(\text{CO}_{2}) + 4 \Delta_{f}H^{\circ}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})] - [2 \Delta_{f}H^{\circ}(\text{CH}_{4}) + 4 \Delta_{f}H^{\circ}(\text{O}_{2})]$

Substituting the given values:

$\Delta_{r}H^{\circ} = [2(-393.5) + 4(-285.8)] - [2(-74.8) + 4(0)]$

$\Delta_{r}H^{\circ} = [-787.0 - 1143.2] - [-149.6]$

$\Delta_{r}H^{\circ} = -1930.2 + 149.6 = -1780.6 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $-1780.6$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For an ideal gas undergoing an isothermal change, there is
options: an increase in Internal energy of the system and heat absorbed by the system is greater than the work done on the system
no change in Internal energy of the system and heat absorbed by the system is equal to the work done by the system
no change in Internal energy of the system and heat released by the system is equal to the work done by the system
a decrease in Internal energy of the system and heat released by the system is equal to the work done by the system
questions.solution:
For an ideal gas, the internal energy depends only on its temperature.

In an isothermal process, the temperature remains constant ($\Delta T = 0$).

Therefore, the change in internal energy is zero ($\Delta U = 0$).

According to the first law of thermodynamics:

$\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$

Substituting $\Delta U = 0$, we get:

$\Delta Q = \Delta W$

This implies that the heat absorbed by the system ($\Delta Q$) is equal to the work done by the system ($\Delta W$).

Answer: no change in Internal energy of the system and heat absorbed by the system is equal to the work done by the system

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Ozone is formed by the reaction
$\text{O}_{2(g)} + \text{O}_{(g)} \rightarrow \text{O}_{3(g)},\ \Delta H = -107.2\ kJ$.
Given O=O bond energy is 498.0 kJ $\text{mol}^{-1}$, the average bond energy of ozone is:
questions.solution:
The enthalpy of the reaction is given by the difference between the sum of bond energies of reactants and products.

$\Delta H = \sum \text{BE(reactants)} - \sum \text{BE(products)}$

For the given reaction $\text{O}_{2(g)} + \text{O}_{(g)} \rightarrow \text{O}_{3(g)}$:

$\Delta H = \text{BE(O=O)} - 2 \times \text{BE(O-O in O}_3)$

Substituting the given values:

$-107.2 = 498.0 - 2 \times \text{BE(O-O in O}_3)$

$2 \times \text{BE(O-O in O}_3) = 498.0 + 107.2$

$2 \times \text{BE(O-O in O}_3) = 605.2$

$\text{BE(O-O in O}_3) = \dfrac{605.2}{2} = 302.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $302.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ for a reaction are 35.5 kJ $\text{mol}^{-1}$ and 83.6 J $\text{K}^{-1}$ respectively. Assuming that $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ do not vary with temperature, the reaction is spontaneous when:
questions.solution:
For a reaction to be spontaneous, the change in Gibbs free energy must be negative, $\Delta G \lt 0$.

Using the Gibbs free energy equation:

$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$

For spontaneity:

$\Delta H - T\Delta S \lt 0$

$T \gt \dfrac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}$

Given values are:

$\Delta H = 35.5 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1} = 35500 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$

$\Delta S = 83.6 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$

Substituting the values:

$T \gt \dfrac{35500}{83.6}$

$T \gt 424.64 \text{ K}$

Therefore, the reaction is spontaneous when $T \gt 425 \text{ K}$.

Answer: $T \gt 425\ K$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The heat of combustion of carbon to $\text{CO}_2$ is -393.5 kJ $\text{mol}^{-1}$.
The heat released on the formation of 35.2 g of $\text{CO}_2$ by combustion of C is:
questions.solution:
The combustion reaction of carbon is given by:

$\text{C(s)} + \text{O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{CO}_2\text{(g)} \quad \Delta H = -393.5\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

Molar mass of $\text{CO}_2 = 12 + 2 \times 16 = 44\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$

Number of moles of $\text{CO}_2$ formed $= \dfrac{35.2}{44} = 0.8\ \text{mol}$

Enthalpy change for the formation of $0.8\ \text{mol}$ of $\text{CO}_2 = 0.8 \times (-393.5\ \text{kJ}) = -314.8\ \text{kJ}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the heat released (enthalpy change) is approximately $-315\ \text{kJ}$.

Answer: $-315\ \text{kJ}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The enthalpy change accompanying the freezing of 18 g of water at $5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to ice at $-5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is:
[Given: $\Delta H_{(\text {fusion })}=6 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C} ; \quad C_p\left(H_2 \mathrm{O}, l\right)=75.3 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} ; \quad C_p\left(H_2 \mathrm{O}, s\right)=36.8 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ ]
questions.solution:
The process of freezing 18 g (1 mole) of water at $5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to ice at $-5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ can be broken down into three steps:

Cooling 1 mole of liquid water from $5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
$\Delta H_1 = n C_p(l) \Delta T = 1 \times 75.3 \times (0 - 5) \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~kJ} = -0.3765 \mathrm{~kJ}$

Phase change of 1 mole of liquid water at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to ice at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
$\Delta H_2 = -\Delta H_{\text{fusion}} = -6.0 \mathrm{~kJ}$

Cooling 1 mole of ice from $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $-5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
$\Delta H_3 = n C_p(s) \Delta T = 1 \times 36.8 \times (-5 - 0) \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~kJ} = -0.184 \mathrm{~kJ}$

Total enthalpy change $\Delta H = \Delta H_1 + \Delta H_2 + \Delta H_3 = -0.3765 - 6.0 - 0.184 = -6.5605 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$.

Answer: $-6.56 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ were found to be both positive for a reversible reaction at temperature ' T '. If the equilibrium temperature is $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{o}}$, the reaction will be spontaneous when
options: $T_o$ should be double than that of T
questions.solution:
For a reaction to be spontaneous, the change in Gibbs free energy must be negative, i.e., $\Delta G \lt 0$.

The relationship between Gibbs free energy, enthalpy, and entropy is given by the equation $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$.

At equilibrium, $\Delta G = 0$, which implies $\Delta H - T_o\Delta S = 0$. Therefore, the equilibrium temperature is $T_o = \dfrac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}$.

For the reaction to be spontaneous, $\Delta H - T\Delta S \lt 0$.

Since $\Delta H \gt 0$ and $\Delta S \gt 0$, we have $\Delta H \lt T\Delta S$, which simplifies to $T \gt \dfrac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}$.

Substituting the expression for $T_o$, we get $T \gt T_o$.

Answer: $T\gt T_o$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: When the combustion of one molecule of liquid heptane is carried out at a constant temperature ' $T$ ', the difference between $\Delta H^o$ and $\Delta U^o$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
The combustion reaction of liquid heptane ($C_{7}H_{16}$) is given by:

$C_{7}H_{16}(l) + 11O_{2}(g) \rightarrow 7CO_{2}(g) + 8H_{2}O(l)$

The relationship between enthalpy change ($\Delta H^{o}$) and internal energy change ($\Delta U^{o}$) is given by the equation:

$\Delta H^{o} = \Delta U^{o} + \Delta n_{g}RT$

where $\Delta n_{g}$ is the change in the number of moles of gaseous species in the reaction.

Calculating $\Delta n_{g}$:

$\Delta n_{g} = \sum n_{g, products} - \sum n_{g, reactants}$

$\Delta n_{g} = 7 - 11 = -4$

Substituting this value into the equation:

$\Delta H^{o} = \Delta U^{o} - 4RT$

Rearranging the terms to find the difference $\Delta H^{o} - \Delta U^{o}$:

$\Delta H^{o} - \Delta U^{o} = -4RT$

Alternatively, rearranging to find $\Delta U^{o} - \Delta H^{o}$:

$\Delta U^{o} - \Delta H^{o} = 4RT$

Answer: $\Delta U^o-\Delta H^o=4 R T$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a hypothetical chemical reaction $\mathrm{A}_2+3 \mathrm{~B}_2+$ Heat $----\rightarrow 2 \mathrm{AB}_3$, which one of the following combinations of state variables would support the spontaneity of the reaction at a particular temperature?
questions.solution:
The given reaction is $\mathrm{A}_{2} + 3\mathrm{B}_{2} + \text{Heat} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{AB}_{3}$.

Since the reaction absorbs heat, it is endothermic, which implies $\Delta \mathrm{H} \gt 0$.

The spontaneity of a reaction is determined by the Gibbs free energy change, $\Delta \mathrm{G} = \Delta \mathrm{H} - \mathrm{T}\Delta \mathrm{S}$. A reaction is spontaneous if $\Delta \mathrm{G} \lt 0$.

For an endothermic reaction ($\Delta \mathrm{H} \gt 0$) to be spontaneous ($\Delta \mathrm{G} \lt 0$), the term $-\mathrm{T}\Delta \mathrm{S}$ must be negative and have a larger magnitude than $\Delta \mathrm{H}$. This requires $\Delta \mathrm{S} \gt 0$.

Comparing this with the given options, the combination $\Delta \mathrm{H} \gt 0$, $\Delta \mathrm{S} \gt 0$, and $\Delta \mathrm{G} \lt 0$ satisfies the condition for spontaneity.

Answer: $\Delta \mathrm{H}\gt 0, \Delta \mathrm{~S}\gt 0, \Delta \mathrm{G} \lt 0$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For the reaction $\text{A}_2 + \text{B}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{AB}$, $\Delta H_f$ (AB) $= -400 \text{ kJ/mol}$. The bond dissociation enthalpies of $\text{A}_2$, $\text{B}_2$ and $\text{AB}$ are in the ratio 1 : 0.75 : 1. What is the bond dissociation enthalpy of $\text{B}_2$ in kJ/mol?
questions.solution:
$\Delta H_{rxn} = 2 \times \Delta H_f(AB) = 2 \times (-400) = -800$ kJ/mol

Let $BE_{A_2} = x$, $BE_{B_2} = 0.75x$, $BE_{AB} = x$

$\Delta H_{rxn} = \sum BE(\text{reactants}) - \sum BE(\text{products})$

$-800 = (x + 0.75x) - 2x = 1.75x - 2x = -0.25x$

$x = \dfrac{-800}{-0.25} = 3200$ kJ/mol

$BE_{B_2} = 0.75 \times 3200 = 2400$ kJ/mol

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The Enthalpy of combustion of 1.0 mole of a reactive metal X at $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and 1.0 bar pressure to form a solid oxide (XO) is $-601.83 \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$. The Internal energy change for this reaction is ______ kJ .
$\left(\mathrm{R}=8.314 \mathrm{J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right)$
questions.solution:
Reaction: $X_{(s)} + \dfrac{1}{2}O_{2(g)} \rightarrow XO_{(s)}$

$\Delta n_g = 0 - \dfrac{1}{2} = -0.5$ mol

$\Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_g RT$

$\Delta U = -601.83 - (-0.5 \times 8.314 \times 10^{-3} \times 300)$

$\Delta U = -601.83 + 1.247 = -600.58$ kJ

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
In the decomposition of limestone to lime, the values of $\Delta H^o$ and $\Delta S^o$ are $+179.1 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ and $160.2 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. Calculate the temperature above which conversion of limestone to lime will be spontaneous, if values of $\Delta H^o$ and $\Delta S^o$ remain unchanged with temperature.
[Assuming pressure 1 bar ]
questions.solution:
The reaction for the decomposition of limestone is $CaCO_{3}(s) \rightarrow CaO(s) + CO_{2}(g)$.

For a reaction to be spontaneous, the Gibbs free energy change $\Delta G^{o}$ must be less than zero. The relationship between $\Delta G^{o}$, $\Delta H^{o}$, and $\Delta S^{o}$ is given by $\Delta G^{o} = \Delta H^{o} - T\Delta S^{o}$.

Setting $\Delta G^{o} \lt 0$ for spontaneity, we have $\Delta H^{o} - T\Delta S^{o} \lt 0$, which implies $T \gt \dfrac{\Delta H^{o}}{\Delta S^{o}}$.

Given $\Delta H^{o} = +179.1 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1} = 179100 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$ and $\Delta S^{o} = 160.2 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$.

Substituting the values into the inequality:

$T \gt \dfrac{179100 \text{ J mol}^{-1}}{160.2 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}}$

$T \gt 1117.977 \text{ K}$

Rounding to the nearest whole number, the temperature above which the reaction becomes spontaneous is approximately $1118 \text{ K}$.

Answer: 1118 K

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Two moles of an ideal gas at 1 bar pressure and 298 K is expanded into vacuum to double the volume. The work done is:
questions.solution:
The expansion of an ideal gas into vacuum is known as free expansion.

In free expansion, the external pressure $P_{ext}$ is equal to $0$ bar.

The formula for work done in a thermodynamic process is given by $W = -\int P_{ext} dV$.

Since $P_{ext} = 0$, the integral becomes $W = -\int 0 dV = 0$.

Therefore, the work done during the expansion of the gas into vacuum is $0$ J.

Answer: 0 J

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The enthalpies of combustion of $\mathrm{H}_2, \mathrm{C}$ (graphite) and $\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_6(\mathrm{~g})$ are $-286.0,-394.0$ and $-1560.0 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and 1 atm pressure. The enthalpy of formation of ethane is:
questions.solution:
The combustion reactions for the given substances are:
1) $\mathrm{H}_2(g) + \dfrac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(l)$, $\Delta H_1 = -286.0 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
2) $\mathrm{C}(s) + \mathrm{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2(g)$, $\Delta H_2 = -394.0 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
3) $\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_6(g) + \dfrac{7}{2} \mathrm{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CO}_2(g) + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(l)$, $\Delta H_3 = -1560.0 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

The formation reaction for ethane is:
2$\mathrm{C}(s) + 3\mathrm{H}_2(g) \rightarrow \mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_6(g)$, $\Delta H_f = ?$

Using Hess's Law, we can express the formation reaction as:
$\Delta H_f = 2 \times (\Delta H_2) + 3 \times (\Delta H_1) - (\Delta H_3)$

Substituting the given values:
$\Delta H_f = 2(-394.0) + 3(-286.0) - (-1560.0)$
$\Delta H_f = -788.0 - 858.0 + 1560.0$
$\Delta H_f = -1646.0 + 1560.0$
$\Delta H_f = -86.0 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $-86.0 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Given that the standard enthalpy of combustion of $\mathrm{C}_{(\mathrm{S})}$ and $\mathrm{CS}_2(\mathrm{l})$ are -393.3 and $-1108.76 \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$ respectively and the standard enthalpy of formation of $\mathrm{CS}_2$ is $128.02 \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$. What is $\Delta H_f^0$ of $\mathrm{SO}_2$ ?
questions.solution:
The combustion reactions are given as follows:

1. $\mathrm{C}_{(\mathrm{s})} + \mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(\mathrm{g})}$, $\Delta H_1 = -393.3 \text{ kJ/mol}$

2. $\mathrm{CS}_{2(\mathrm{l})} + 3\mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(\mathrm{g})} + 2\mathrm{SO}_{2(\mathrm{g})}$, $\Delta H_2 = -1108.76 \text{ kJ/mol}$

The enthalpy of formation of $\mathrm{CS}_{2(\mathrm{l})}$ is given by the reaction:

3. $\mathrm{C}_{(\mathrm{s})} + 2\mathrm{S}_{(\mathrm{s})} \rightarrow \mathrm{CS}_{2(\mathrm{l})}$, $\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{CS}_2) = 128.02 \text{ kJ/mol}$

The enthalpy of combustion of $\mathrm{CS}_{2(\mathrm{l})}$ can be expressed in terms of enthalpies of formation:

$\Delta H_2 = [\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{CO}_2) + 2\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{SO}_2)] - [\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{CS}_2) + 3\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{O}_2)]$

Since $\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{CO}_2) = \Delta H_1 = -393.3 \text{ kJ/mol}$ and $\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{O}_2) = 0$, we substitute the values:

$-1108.76 = [-393.3 + 2\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{SO}_2)] - [128.02 + 0]$

$-1108.76 = -393.3 + 2\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{SO}_2) - 128.02$

$-1108.76 = -521.32 + 2\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{SO}_2)$

$2\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{SO}_2) = -1108.76 + 521.32 = -587.44$

$\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{SO}_2) = -293.72 \text{ kJ/mol}$

Answer: $-293.72 \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
0.4 g of Propane burns completely at 300 K in a bomb calorimeter. The temperature of the calorimeter and surrounding water rises by $0.4^0 \mathrm{C}$.
If the heat capacity of the calorimeter and contents is $24 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$ what is the Enthalpy for the reaction?
(Assume that propane gas shows ideal behaviour).
questions.solution:
The combustion reaction of propane is given by: $C_{3}H_{8}(g) + 5O_{2}(g) \rightarrow 3CO_{2}(g) + 4H_{2}O(l)$.

The heat released in the bomb calorimeter is $q_{v} = C \times \Delta T$, where $C = 24 \text{ kJ K}^{-1}$ and $\Delta T = 0.4 \text{ K}$.

$q_{v} = 24 \times 0.4 = 9.6 \text{ kJ}$.

The number of moles of propane ($C_{3}H_{8}$) is $n = \dfrac{0.4 \text{ g}}{44 \text{ g mol}^{-1}} = \dfrac{0.4}{44} \text{ mol} = \dfrac{1}{110} \text{ mol}$.

The internal energy change for the combustion of 1 mole of propane is $\Delta U = -\dfrac{q_{v}}{n} = -9.6 \times 110 = -1056 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

The enthalpy change is given by $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_{g}RT$, where $\Delta n_{g} = (3 - 1 - 5) = -3$.

Using $R = 8.314 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kJ K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$ and $T = 300 \text{ K}$:

$\Delta H = -1056 + (-3) \times (8.314 \times 10^{-3}) \times 300 = -1056 - 7.4826 = -1063.4826 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Rounding to one decimal place, we get $\Delta H \approx -1063.5 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Answer: $-1063.5 \mathrm{~kJ}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a reaction $\mathrm{X}_2(\mathrm{l})+\mathrm{Y}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \leftrightharpoons 2 \mathrm{XY}(\mathrm{g})$, the $\Delta \mathrm{H}^0$ and $\Delta \mathrm{S}^0$ are $+29.3 \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$ and $104.1 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ respectively at 298 K . Find the free energy change in $\mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$.
questions.solution:
The Gibbs free energy change $\Delta G^0$ is given by the relation $\Delta G^0 = \Delta H^0 - T\Delta S^0$.

Given values are $\Delta H^0 = 29.3 \text{ kJ/mol}$ and $\Delta S^0 = 104.1 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1} = 0.1041 \text{ kJ K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$ at $T = 298 \text{ K}$.

Substituting these values into the equation:

$\Delta G^0 = 29.3 \text{ kJ/mol} - (298 \text{ K} \times 0.1041 \text{ kJ K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1})$

$\Delta G^0 = 29.3 - 31.0218$

$\Delta G^0 = -1.7218 \text{ kJ/mol}$.

The magnitude of the free energy change is approximately $1.72 \text{ kJ/mol}$.

Answer: $1.72$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
At 300 K , one mole of ideal gas in thermal contact with surrounding expands isothermally from 1.0 L to 2.0 L against a constant pressure of 3.0 atm. In this process the change in entropy of surrounding $\left(\Delta S_{\text {surr }}\right)$ in J/K.
$(1 \mathrm{~L} \mathrm{~atm}=101.3 \mathrm{~J})$
questions.solution:
$\Delta S_{\text {surrounding }}=\frac{q_{\text {surrounding }}}{T}=\frac{-q_{\text {system }}}{T}=\frac{W_{\text {system }}}{T}$
(For isothermal process, $\Delta U=0, \because q=-W$ )
$\begin{aligned} \\ & W_{\text {system }}=-P_{\text {ext }}\left(V_f-V_i\right) \\ \\ & \quad=-3(2-1)=-3 \mathrm{~L} \mathrm{~atm} \\ \\ & \begin{aligned} \\ \therefore \Delta S_{\text {surrounding }}= & \frac{-3}{300} \mathrm{~L} \mathrm{~atm}=-0.01 \mathrm{Latm} \\ \\ & =-0.01 \times 101.3 \mathrm{~J}=-1.013 \mathrm{~J} \\ \end{aligned} \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: One mole of an ideal gas for which $C_V=\frac{3}{2} R$ is heated reversibly at constant pressure of 1 atm from $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C} . \Delta H$ will be
questions.solution:
We know that,
$\begin{aligned} \\ & C_P=C_V+R \\ \\ & C_P=\frac{3}{2} R+R=\frac{5}{2} R \\ \end{aligned}$
At constant pressure, heat absorb by one mole of gas $\left(q_p\right)$
$\begin{aligned} \\ & =n C_p \Delta T=1 \times \frac{5}{2}[100-25] R \\ \\ & =1 \times \frac{5}{2} \times 1.987 \times 75 \\ \\ q_p & =372.56 \mathrm{cal} \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Given the bond enthalpies of $\mathrm{N} \equiv \mathrm{N}$ is $946 \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$. $\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H}$ is $435 \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol}, \mathrm{N}-\mathrm{N}$ is $159 \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$ and $\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{H}$ is $389 \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$, heat of formation of hydrazine in the gas phase (in $\mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$) is
questions.solution:
The reaction to form hydrazine is as follows
$\mathrm{N}_2(g)+2 \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H}(\mathrm{~g}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{H}_4(g)$

$\begin{aligned} \Delta_r H^{\circ}=\Delta_f H^{\circ}\left(\mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{H}_4\right)=\Sigma \mathrm{BE}(\text { reactant }) -\Sigma \mathrm{BE} \text { (product) }\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}=[B \cdot E(N \equiv N+ & 2 B \cdot E \cdot(H-H)] -[B E(N-N)+4(B E)(N-H)]\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} & =[946+2(435)]-[159+4 \times 389] \\ & =101 \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
At Constant volume, the heat required to raise the temperature of $4.48 \mathrm{~L}$ of an ideal gas at STP by $15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is 12.0 calories.
The $\mathrm{C_p}$ of the gas is _____________ 
$(\mathrm{R}=2 \mathrm{~Cal} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1})$
questions.solution:
At STP, the volume of 1 mole of an ideal gas is $22.4 \text{ L}$.

The number of moles $n$ in $4.48 \text{ L}$ is given by $n = \dfrac{4.48}{22.4} = 0.2 \text{ mol}$.

The heat required at constant volume is given by $q_v = n C_v \Delta T$.

Given $q_v = 12 \text{ cal}$, $n = 0.2 \text{ mol}$, and $\Delta T = 15^{\circ} \text{C}$, we have $12 = 0.2 \times C_v \times 15$.

$12 = 3 \times C_v \Rightarrow C_v = 4 \text{ cal mol}^{-1} \text{ K}^{-1}$.

Using the relation $C_p - C_v = R$, where $R = 2 \text{ cal mol}^{-1} \text{ K}^{-1}$:

$C_p = C_v + R = 4 + 2 = 6 \text{ cal mol}^{-1} \text{ K}^{-1}$.

Answer: 6 cal

questions.q: The correct option for free expansion of an ideal gas under adiabatic condition is:
questions.solution:
Free expansion of an ideal gas occurs against vacuum, which implies that the external pressure $P_{ext} = 0$.

The work done in the process is given by $w = -\int P_{ext} dV$. Since $P_{ext} = 0$, the work done $w = 0$.

The process is stated to be adiabatic, which means there is no heat exchange with the surroundings, so $q = 0$.

According to the first law of thermodynamics, $\Delta U = q + w$. Substituting $q = 0$ and $w = 0$, we get $\Delta U = 0$.

For an ideal gas, the internal energy $U$ is a function of temperature only, i.e., $U = f(T)$. Therefore, $\Delta U = n C_v \Delta T$. Since $\Delta U = 0$ and $n, C_v \neq 0$, it follows that $\Delta T = 0$.

Thus, for free expansion of an ideal gas under adiabatic conditions, $q = 0$, $w = 0$, and $\Delta T = 0$.

Answer: $\mathrm{q}=0, \quad \Delta \mathrm{T}=0, \quad \mathrm{w}=0$

$\Delta H^{\circ}_{r} = \sum \Delta H^{\circ}_{f}(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H^{\circ}_{f}(\text{reactants})$

Given $\Delta H^{\circ}_{f}(\mathrm{NO}_2) = 16.0 \text{ kcal mol}^{-1}$ and $\Delta H^{\circ}_{f}(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4) = 4.0 \text{ kcal mol}^{-1}$, we substitute these values into the equation:

$\Delta H^{\circ}_{r} = \Delta H^{\circ}_{f}(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4) - 2 \times \Delta H^{\circ}_{f}(\mathrm{NO}_2)$

$\Delta H^{\circ}_{r} = 4.0 - 2 \times 16.0$

$\Delta H^{\circ}_{r} = 4.0 - 32.0$

$\Delta H^{\circ}_{r} = -28.0 \text{ kcal}$

Answer: $-28$ k cal

questions.q:
5.0 moles of an Ideal gas at 3.0 atm pressure and $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is compressed isothermally to half its volume by application of an external pressure of $3.5 \mathrm{~atm}$. What is the amount of work done (in joules) on the gas?
Given: $1 \mathrm{~L} \mathrm{~atm}=101.3 \mathrm{~J}: \mathrm{R}=0.082 \mathrm{~L} \mathrm{~atm} \mathrm{~K}{ }^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
questions.solution:
The initial state of the gas is given by $n = 5.0$ mol, $P_1 = 3.0$ atm, and $T = 27^{\circ}C = 300$ K.

Using the ideal gas law $PV = nRT$, the initial volume $V_1$ is calculated as:

$V_1 = \dfrac{nRT}{P_1} = \dfrac{5.0 \times 0.082 \times 300}{3.0} = 41$ L.

The gas is compressed isothermally to half its volume, so the final volume $V_2$ is:

$V_2 = \dfrac{V_1}{2} = \dfrac{41}{2} = 20.5$ L.

The change in volume $\Delta V = V_2 - V_1 = 20.5 - 41 = -20.5$ L.

The work done on the gas during an irreversible isothermal compression against a constant external pressure $P_{ext}$ is given by $W = -P_{ext} \Delta V$.

Given $P_{ext} = 3.5$ atm, the work done is:

$W = -3.5 \times (-20.5) = 71.75$ L atm.

Converting the work into Joules using the conversion factor $1$ L atm $= 101.3$ J:

$W = 71.75 \times 101.3 = 7268.275$ J.

Rounding to one decimal place, the work done is $7268.3$ J.

Answer: 7268.3

What is the bond enthalpy of $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}$ bond in Methane?
questions.solution:
The formation reaction of methane is given by: $\text{C(s)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_4\text{(g)}$. The enthalpy of this reaction is $\Delta_f H^{\circ} = -74.8 \text{ kJ/mol}$.

The atomization process involves the sublimation of carbon and the dissociation of hydrogen molecules:
1. $\text{C(s)} \rightarrow \text{C(g)}$, $\Delta H_1 = 719.6 \text{ kJ/mol}$
2. $2\text{H}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow 4\text{H(g)}$, $\Delta H_2 = 2 \times 436 = 872 \text{ kJ/mol}$

The total energy required to break all bonds in $\text{CH}_4$ to form gaseous atoms is the enthalpy of atomization of methane, $\Delta_{at} H^{\circ}$:
$\Delta_{at} H^{\circ} = \Delta H_1 + \Delta H_2 - \Delta_f H^{\circ}$
$\Delta_{at} H^{\circ} = 719.6 + 872 - (-74.8) = 719.6 + 872 + 74.8 = 1666.4 \text{ kJ/mol}$.

Since methane ($\text{CH}_4$) contains four $\text{C-H}$ bonds, the bond enthalpy of a single $\text{C-H}$ bond is:
$\text{Bond Enthalpy} = \dfrac{1666.4}{4} = 416.6 \text{ kJ/mol}$.

Answer: 416.6 kJ

questions.solution:
The reaction for the cyclic polymerization of ethyne to benzene is given by: $3C_{2}H_{2}(g) \rightarrow C_{6}H_{6}(l)$.

The standard Gibbs free energy change for the reaction, $\Delta G^{0}_{rxn}$, is calculated as:
$\Delta G^{0}_{rxn} = \sum \Delta G^{0}_{f}(products) - \sum \Delta G^{0}_{f}(reactants)$
$\Delta G^{0}_{rxn} = \Delta G^{0}_{f}(C_{6}H_{6}) - 3 \times \Delta G^{0}_{f}(C_{2}H_{2})$
$\Delta G^{0}_{rxn} = 1.24 \times 10^{5} - 3 \times (2.09 \times 10^{5})$
$\Delta G^{0}_{rxn} = 1.24 \times 10^{5} - 6.27 \times 10^{5} = -5.03 \times 10^{5} \text{ J/mol}$.

The relationship between $\Delta G^{0}$ and the equilibrium constant $K$ is given by $\Delta G^{0} = -RT \ln K$.
Given $T = 27^{\circ}C = 300 \text{ K}$ and $R = 8.314 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$.
$-5.03 \times 10^{5} = -8.314 \times 300 \times \ln K$
$\ln K = \dfrac{5.03 \times 10^{5}}{8.314 \times 300}$
$\ln K = \dfrac{503000}{2494.2} \approx 201.667$.

$K = e^{201.667} \approx 1.429 \times 10^{87} \approx 1.429 \times 10^{88}$.

Answer: $1.429\times10^{88}$

Let the bond dissociation energies of $\mathrm{A}_2$, $\mathrm{B}_2$, and $\mathrm{AB}$ be $2x$, $x$, and $2x$ respectively, based on the given ratio $2:1:2$.

Substituting these into the enthalpy equation: $-400 = \left( \dfrac{1}{2}(2x) + \dfrac{1}{2}(x) \right) - (2x)$.

The decomposition reaction of nitrous oxide is: $2N_{2}O(g) \rightarrow 2N_{2}(g) + O_{2}(g)$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Which of the following are not path functions?
I. $H-T S$
II. W
II. $q$
IV. $q+W$
questions.solution:
A path function is a property whose value depends on the path taken to reach a state, whereas a state function depends only on the initial and final states of the system.

The term $H - TS$ represents the Gibbs free energy, $G = H - TS$. Since $H$, $T$, and $S$ are all state functions, their combination $G$ is also a state function.

Work ($W$) and heat ($q$) are well-known path functions as they depend on the process by which the system changes state.

According to the first law of thermodynamics, $q + W = \Delta U$. Since the internal energy change $\Delta U$ is a state function, the sum $q + W$ is a state function.

Therefore, the quantities that are not path functions (i.e., they are state functions) are I ($H - TS$) and IV ($q + W$).

Answer: I and IV

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The relation between work done in reversible and irreversible process is
questions.solution:
For a given change in state of a system, the work done in a reversible process is the maximum work that can be obtained from the system during expansion, or the minimum work that must be done on the system during compression.

In an irreversible process, the system undergoes a spontaneous change where the external pressure is not balanced by the internal pressure at every instant, leading to a loss of energy as heat due to friction or turbulence.

For expansion, the work done by the system in a reversible process is greater than the work done in an irreversible process, i.e., $|W_{\text{rev}}| \gt |W_{\text{irr}}|$.

Since work done by the system is conventionally negative and work done on the system is positive, in terms of magnitude for expansion, $W_{\text{rev}}$ is the maximum work, implying $W_{\text{irr}} \lt W_{\text{rev}}$ when considering the algebraic values of work done by the system.

Answer: $W_{\text {irr }} \lt W_{\text {rev }}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: In which of the following changes, entropy decreases?
questions.solution:
Entropy is a measure of the randomness or disorder of a system. A decrease in entropy corresponds to a transition from a more disordered state to a more ordered state.

Rusting of iron involves the reaction of iron with oxygen and water to form hydrated iron(III) oxide. This process increases the number of particles and the complexity of the system, leading to an increase in entropy.

Melting of ice is a phase transition from solid to liquid. The liquid state has higher molecular mobility and disorder than the solid state, so entropy increases.

Vaporisation of camphor is a phase transition from solid to gas. The gaseous state has significantly higher entropy than the solid state due to increased molecular freedom and volume, so entropy increases.

Crystallisation of sucrose from a solution involves the transition of solute molecules from a disordered state in the liquid solvent to a highly ordered, repeating lattice structure in the solid crystal. This transition results in a decrease in the randomness of the system, hence entropy decreases.

Answer: Crystallisation of sucrose from solution

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The difference between heat capacity at constant pressure and heat capacity at constant volume is
questions.solution:
For an ideal gas, the enthalpy $H$ is defined as $H = U + PV$.

Differentiating with respect to temperature $T$ at constant pressure, we have $\left( \dfrac{\partial H}{\partial T} \right)_P = \left( \dfrac{\partial U}{\partial T} \right)_P + P \left( \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial T} \right)_P$.

By definition, $C_P = \left( \dfrac{\partial H}{\partial T} \right)_P$ and $C_V = \left( \dfrac{\partial U}{\partial T} \right)_V$. For an ideal gas, $U$ depends only on temperature, so $\left( \dfrac{\partial U}{\partial T} \right)_P = \left( \dfrac{\partial U}{\partial T} \right)_V = C_V$.

Using the ideal gas equation $PV = nRT$, for one mole ($n=1$), $PV = RT$. Differentiating with respect to $T$ at constant pressure gives $P \left( \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial T} \right)_P = R$.

Substituting these into the enthalpy derivative equation, we get $C_P = C_V + R$, which implies $C_P - C_V = R$.

Answer: $R$
